books.title: I. The Empire of the Romans
books.subtitle: The Eastern Roman Empire
books.text:
The Eastern Roman Empire, commonly but somewhat misleadingly known today as the Byzantine Empire, is the surviving continuation of the Roman Empire of antiquity. Its inhabitants call themselves Romans (Rhomaioi), their state the Empire of the Romans, and their capital New Rome. The term “Byzantine Empire” was introduced by later historians, derived from Byzantion, the ancient Greek settlement upon which Constantinople was built. The distinction is more than academic. The empire did not emerge as a successor state claiming Roman heritage. It was Rome, transformed by centuries of history, Christianity, and the gradual displacement of Latin by Greek as its principal language.

Following the collapse of imperial authority in Western Europe during the fifth century, the Eastern Empire continued to flourish. Its emperors ruled territories stretching from the Balkans to Syria and Egypt, and at times reconquered substantial parts of Italy, Africa, and Spain. Roman law was codified under Emperor Justinian I, establishing a legal tradition that would profoundly influence European civilisation. Its armies, bureaucracy, taxation, diplomacy, and sophisticated monetary system allowed the empire to survive enemies and catastrophes that destroyed countless other states. Roman power was never merely a matter of military strength. More often, it was the ability to organise resources, exploit divisions among enemies, and preserve institutions across generations.

Over the centuries, the empire developed a distinctive civilisation combining Roman statecraft, Greek philosophy, and Orthodox Christianity. Constantinople became one of the great centres of Christian theology, scholarship, architecture, and artistic achievement. Roman missionaries and ecclesiastical institutions played a formative role in the Christianisation of the Slavic world, from Bulgaria and Serbia to the lands of Kyivan Rus'. The imperial court exercised an influence far beyond the empire's frontiers. Even rulers who fought against Constantinople frequently sought its titles, marriages, ceremonial recognition, and religious legitimacy. Its greatest victories were sometimes achieved without an army ever leaving the capital.

Yet this civilisation was neither uniformly prosperous nor perpetually united. Religious controversies, aristocratic rivalries, provincial rebellions, and foreign invasions periodically brought the empire close to destruction. The rise of Islam deprived it of some of its richest territories, while the Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071 accelerated the loss of much of Anatolia. The most devastating blow, however, came from fellow Christians. In 1204, the Fourth Crusade captured and plundered Constantinople, replacing the Roman government with a Latin Empire. Exiled Roman rulers preserved imperial institutions in several successor states, most notably Nicaea. Against considerable odds, Michael VIII Palaiologos recovered Constantinople in 1261 and restored the empire.

The restoration was a remarkable achievement, but it did not restore the resources upon which Roman greatness had rested. The recovered capital was impoverished, the provinces fragmented, and maritime commerce increasingly controlled by Italian merchant republics. Civil wars and successive epidemics further weakened the state, while new powers emerged upon its former territories. By 1452, the empire possesses little more than Constantinople, portions of the Peloponnese, and a few remaining dependencies. Nevertheless, its emperor still claims the inheritance of Augustus and Constantine the Great. Behind the diminished frontiers survives an extraordinary accumulation of laws, institutions, diplomatic relationships, religious authority, and historical memory. The Roman Empire has been reduced to a shadow of its former greatness. Whether that shadow must finally disappear remains another question.

books.title: II. The Queen of Cities
books.subtitle: Constantinople
books.text:
Few cities in human history have occupied a position comparable to Constantinople. Founded as the Greek settlement of Byzantion in the seventh century BC, the city was refounded by Constantine the Great in AD 330 as a new imperial capital. Its geography was exceptional: a defensible peninsula commanding the Bosphorus, the narrow maritime passage linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean world. Whoever controlled Constantinople could influence the movement of grain, merchants, fleets, and armies between two continents. The city became both a fortress and an imperial command centre, situated at the intersection of Europe and Asia.

For more than a thousand years, Constantinople stood among the greatest cities of the Christian world. Its monumental churches, imperial palaces, libraries, markets, aqueducts, baths, and public squares astonished foreign visitors. At its spiritual centre rose Hagia Sophia, completed under Justinian in 537, whose vast dome seemed to defy the limitations of human construction. The city possessed enormous underground cisterns, complex water infrastructure, and architectural achievements unmatched across much of medieval Europe. Byzantine craftsmanship produced magnificent mosaics, illuminated manuscripts, icons, jewellery, and ceremonial objects. Constantinople was not merely an administrative capital, but a living expression of imperial civilisation.

It was also a remarkably cosmopolitan city. Greek-speaking Romans lived alongside Armenians, Italians, Jews, and merchants from across the Mediterranean and Black Sea. Venetians and Genoese maintained commercial networks and privileged communities, sometimes competing violently with one another and with the imperial government. Across the Golden Horn stood Galata, a fortified Genoese colony whose prosperity contrasted with the empire's declining maritime independence. Latin and Greek Christians traded together even as their churches remained divided. The city was a place of extraordinary wealth and religious devotion, but equally of intrigue, factional conflict, commercial ambition, and occasional popular unrest.

Constantinople's greatest physical asset was its formidable system of fortifications. The Theodosian Walls, constructed in the fifth century, combined a deep moat, outer defences, and successive defensive walls into one of the most sophisticated military systems ever built. The city's maritime approaches were protected by sea walls, while a great iron chain could close access to the Golden Horn. These defences had repeatedly frustrated superior armies. Yet the city of 1452 is no longer the teeming metropolis of earlier centuries. Its population has fallen and gardens and open spaces now occupy areas once densely inhabited. The walls remain immense, but the manpower required to defend them has become increasingly scarce.

To understand Constantinople, however, one must look beyond its walls and monuments. For its inhabitants, the city is a sacred inheritance, protected in popular belief by the Virgin Mary, whose icons accompany processions in times of danger. It is the seat of the Ecumenical Patriarch, the centre of Roman imperial legitimacy, and a symbolic point of reference for Orthodox Christians far beyond its frontiers. Generations have witnessed sieges, epidemics, fires, dynastic struggles, and foreign occupations, yet the city has repeatedly recovered. Its survival has become almost inseparable from its identity. Constantinople is more than a collection of buildings or even the capital of an empire. It is the Queen of Cities—and for many of those living within its walls, the last surviving image of an entire world.

books.title: III. Sunset of an Empire
books.subtitle: The Political Situation, 1402–1452
books.text:
The Roman Empire's decline was neither continuous nor inevitable. Even after the catastrophe of 1204, the Romans recovered their capital and preserved their independence for nearly two further centuries. Yet the fourteenth century proved disastrous. Repeated civil wars exhausted the state, while the Black Death devastated its population and economy. Meanwhile, the Ottomans established themselves in Europe following their crossing of the Dardanelles in the 1350s. Adrianople fell under Ottoman control, the Balkan kingdoms were progressively defeated or subordinated, and Constantinople found itself increasingly surrounded. By the end of the century, the emperors had been reduced to precarious dependence upon Ottoman goodwill.

Then came an extraordinary reversal. In 1402, the conqueror Timur defeated and captured Sultan Bayezid I at Ankara, plunging the Ottoman dynasty into a prolonged struggle for succession. Constantinople, which had endured years of blockade, was granted an unexpected reprieve. Emperor Manuel II exploited the opportunity through diplomacy, recovering territories and securing temporary relief from Ottoman domination. For a generation, the prospect of Roman recovery appeared at least conceivable. Yet the opportunity was never fully realised. Ottoman unity was eventually restored, and the empire lacked the resources to rebuild its former power. In 1422, Constantinople once again faced an Ottoman siege, which it survived.

The following decades witnessed a growing contradiction between Constantinople's cultural vitality and its political impotence. Thessaloniki, once the empire's second city, fell to the Ottomans in 1430 after years under Venetian administration. The imperial court increasingly looked westward for assistance, culminating in the Council of Florence in 1439, where Emperor John VIII accepted a formal reunion between the Orthodox and Catholic Churches. The calculation was political as well as religious: ecclesiastical reconciliation might unlock the military and financial resources of Western Christendom. Yet the agreement provoked intense opposition among clergy, monks, and ordinary Romans. To many, union with Rome threatened the faith and traditions which the empire had struggled for centuries to preserve.

Western intervention nevertheless remained a real possibility. In 1444, a crusading army led by King Władysław III of Poland and Hungary, supported by the formidable Hungarian commander John Hunyadi, marched against the Ottomans. Its destruction at the Battle of Varna, where Władysław was killed, dealt a severe blow to hopes of liberating the Balkans. In 1446, Sultan Murad II invaded the Peloponnese, breaking through the reconstructed Hexamilion Wall that defended the Roman territories of the Morea. Two years later, Hunyadi suffered another major defeat at the Second Battle of Kosovo. The Ottoman state emerged from these conflicts militarily strengthened, while its opponents remained divided by competing dynastic, religious, and commercial interests.

In 1451, the death of Murad II brought his young son Mehmed II to the throne. Initially, the new sultan renewed agreements with several neighbouring powers, but his intentions regarding Constantinople soon became increasingly clear. Construction of the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the European shore of the Bosphorus in 1452 threatened the city's access to the Black Sea. Serbia remained entangled in Ottoman diplomacy, Hungary was recovering from defeat, and Venice and Genoa balanced their commercial interests against the danger of Ottoman expansion. Yet the situation was not without possibilities. The Ottomans faced rivals and obligations across an enormous frontier, while opposition to their rule persisted in the Balkans and Anatolia. Constantinople stood near the centre of a dangerous but fluid political system. Its survival would depend upon whether the Romans could exploit these competing interests before their enemies concentrated overwhelming force against the city.

books.title: IV. Enter the Last Emperor
books.subtitle: Constantine XI Palaiologos Dragases
books.text:
Constantine XI Palaiologos Dragases was born in Constantinople around 1404–1405, the son of Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos and Helena Dragaš, a noblewoman of Serbian origin. His family represented the complicated dynastic world of the late Roman Empire, in which Greek, Serbian, Italian, and other ruling houses had become deeply interconnected through marriage and political necessity. Constantine inherited the name Dragases from his maternal family, a reminder of the close relationship between the Roman imperial house and the Christian aristocracy of the Balkans. By 1452, he is approximately forty-seven or forty-eight years old. He is not a young prince suddenly confronted with catastrophe, but an experienced ruler who has spent much of his life dealing with the empire's decline.

As a younger son, Constantine was not originally expected to inherit the throne. His elder brother John VIII became emperor in 1425, while Constantine was entrusted with military, administrative, and diplomatic responsibilities. He served as regent in Constantinople during periods of his brother's absence and spent much of his career governing Roman territories in the Peloponnese, then known as the Morea. From the imperial centre at Mystras, he confronted rival Latin rulers, ambitious local aristocrats, and the increasingly threatening power of the Ottomans. These experiences gave him a practical understanding of warfare, finance, and government that distinguished him from emperors whose authority rarely extended beyond the palace.

Constantine achieved several notable successes in the Morea, helping to recover territories that had remained under Latin control since the Fourth Crusade. His campaigns expanded Roman authority across much of the Peloponnese, while the reconstruction of the Hexamilion Wall at the Isthmus of Corinth reflected ambitions to establish a defensible frontier. Yet these achievements also revealed the limits of Roman power. In 1444–1446, Constantine extended his influence into central Greece, challenging Ottoman interests and provoking a major response from Sultan Murad II. The Ottoman invasion of 1446 shattered the Hexamilion defences and compelled the Roman rulers of the Morea to submit to tributary obligations. Constantine had demonstrated initiative and considerable military ability, but he had also experienced the consequences of confronting a much more powerful enemy.

The death of John VIII in October 1448 brought Constantine to the imperial throne. His succession was not entirely uncontested: his brother Demetrios possessed ambitions of his own, while their mother Helena played an important role in ensuring Constantine's recognition. He was proclaimed emperor at Mystras on 6 January 1449 and arrived in Constantinople that March. Remarkably, he never received the traditional patriarchal coronation in Hagia Sophia, largely because of the ecclesiastical controversies surrounding union with Rome. He inherited a severely impoverished state, with a treasury incapable of supporting the institutions, military establishments, and ceremonial grandeur traditionally expected of a Roman emperor. Even members of the imperial court increasingly depended upon private wealth to fulfil their responsibilities.

Constantine's personal circumstances reflected the uncertain future of his dynasty. He had married twice and been widowed twice. His first wife, Theodora Tocco, died in 1429, barely a year after their marriage. His second wife, Caterina Gattilusio, a member of the Genoese ruling family of Lesbos, died in 1442. Neither marriage produced a surviving child. Thus, in 1452, the emperor remains unmarried and without a direct heir. Diplomatic efforts to arrange a third marriage have considered princesses from Georgia and Trebizond, as well as Mara Branković, the Serbian princess and widow of Sultan Murad II. Such a marriage would be no mere private affair. It could provide a dowry, strengthen an alliance, influence Ottoman diplomacy, and perhaps secure the future of the Palaiologos dynasty.

The religious divisions of Constantinople present Constantine with another difficult inheritance. The emperor supports the policy of reconciliation with Rome pursued by his brother, recognising that Western military assistance may be essential for the city's survival. Yet many influential Romans regard the Union of Florence as a betrayal of Orthodoxy. Among its critics stands the scholar and monk Gennadios Scholarios, while supporters of union argue that the empire can no longer afford estrangement from the Latin powers. Constantine must navigate these divisions without allowing them to destroy the unity of the city. His position is further complicated by rivalries among aristocratic families, the political influence of the clergy, and the competing interests of Venetian and Genoese merchants. He must govern a society that is highly educated, deeply religious, proud of its inheritance, and far from politically united.

Contemporary accounts generally portray Constantine as courageous, energetic, and conscious of his responsibilities, though these qualities should not obscure the limitations of his position or the political miscalculations of his earlier career. His closest associates include the diplomat and historian George Sphrantzes, while powerful figures such as the Grand Duke Loukas Notaras command resources and influence essential to the empire's survival. Constantine's brothers Demetrios and Thomas govern the remaining Roman territories of the Morea, but their rivalry complicates hopes of coordinated action. Around him stands a diminished yet still functioning imperial government, supported by administrators, soldiers, merchants, churchmen, and foreign adventurers. He possesses neither the armies of Justinian nor the wealth of Basil II. What remains to him is the authority of the Roman throne, the extraordinary city entrusted to his care, and whatever advantages his judgement can create from an increasingly dangerous situation.

books.title: V. The Fall of Constantinople
books.subtitle: History, Possibility, and the Roads Not Taken
books.text:
In our historical timeline, Constantinople fell to the Ottoman army of Sultan Mehmed II on 29 May 1453, following a siege lasting nearly two months. Constantine XI died during the final assault, becoming the last reigning emperor of a state whose origins reached back to ancient Rome. The city was subjected to plunder, thousands of its inhabitants were killed, enslaved, or displaced, and Hagia Sophia was transformed into a mosque. Mehmed claimed the inheritance of Roman imperial sovereignty, making Constantinople the centre of an expanding Ottoman imperial project. The Roman Empire had finally ceased to exist as an independent political power.

The consequences were profound, although they are sometimes oversimplified. The conquest consolidated Ottoman power on both sides of the Bosphorus and transformed the strategic balance of southeastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean. The new Ottoman capital would eventually become one of the greatest cities of the Islamic world, while Orthodox Christians continued their religious and communal life under Ottoman sovereignty. In the West, the fall intensified concern over Ottoman expansion and strengthened interest in the political and intellectual inheritance of the ancient Greeks and Romans. Greek scholars had already contributed to the Italian Renaissance before 1453, but the conquest accelerated the movement of people, manuscripts, and knowledge westward. For the Orthodox world, Constantinople's loss became an enduring religious and historical trauma, influencing the ambitions and identities of later powers, including Muscovy.

Yet it would be a mistake to interpret the events of 1453 as a foregone conclusion. Constantinople remained an extraordinarily defensible position, protected by formidable walls, difficult maritime approaches, and a population whose political and religious identity had survived repeated disasters. The defenders were badly outnumbered, but the Ottomans still faced formidable logistical and military challenges. During the historical siege, Roman and allied soldiers repelled repeated assaults, repaired damaged fortifications, and achieved notable successes at sea. Mehmed's eventual victory depended not merely upon superior numbers, but upon preparation, artillery, naval operations, persistent pressure, and the exhaustion of the defenders. For much of the siege, the city continued to resist effectively.

Nor was the wider political situation entirely hopeless. Ottoman power, although formidable, was neither limitless nor uncontested. Hungary, Venice, Genoa, the Balkan states, and the remaining powers of Anatolia and the Black Sea possessed interests that could potentially have been mobilised against Mehmed. Constantinople's rulers had repeatedly survived similar crises through diplomacy, alliances, deception, financial concessions, and skilful exploitation of their enemies' divisions. Foreign volunteers who came to defend the city were motivated by religion, honour, commercial interests, personal ambition, and genuine calculations about the possibility of resistance. The odds were undoubtedly against the Romans, but military history contains no shortage of great powers whose apparently inevitable victories ended in unexpected failure.

Saving Constantinople begins from this historical reality, but does not assume that the future has already been written. Its purpose is not simply to recreate the final siege, but to explore the choices, constraints, possibilities, and extraordinary individuals who shaped the last years of the Roman Empire. Could better preparations have preserved the city? Could the diplomatic resources of Constantinople have divided its enemies, secured foreign intervention, or transformed the wider balance of power? Could the Roman state have survived another generation—or even experienced a new restoration? Some alternatives are more plausible than others, and every decision carries its costs. History records what happened. It does not establish that nothing else could have happened.
